title: The Great Blockade
summary: Use the bishop to restrain both spare pawns, then force the opposing king away from the squares that trap your own king.

nodes.question: How can White free a king that blocks its own pawn?
nodes.explanation: Begin after ...Kc8. White’s king on a8 blocks its own a7 pawn, and Black keeps the king trapped by controlling b8 and b7.

nodes.question: Why must the black king finally give ground?
nodes.explanation: This position is derived by legal replay after Bh3 in the selected route around 171 seconds. Bh3 blocks h4 while controlling c8, forcing the king to give ground; the sampled source images span the subsequent king moves.

branches.title: Restrain the pawns until the king must move
commentary: Begin after ...Kc8. White’s king on a8 blocks its own a7 pawn, and Black keeps the king trapped by controlling b8 and b7.
Be8 targets d7 and prepares a bishop offer. The piece on e8 is a bishop, despite the caption calling it a king move.
c5 keeps the d7 pawn in place and vacates c7 for the black king.
Bxd7+ removes d7 with check and offers the bishop to the king.
Kc7 declines the bishop, continuing to restrict Ka8.
Be6 controls c8, c4 and h3. White begins restricting both pawn advances without abandoning the king blockade.
h6 is the source’s patient pawn move, preserving more waiting moves than an immediate ...h5.
Bd5 changes the bishop’s diagonal, covering c4 and preparing a return while allowing the king to c8.
Kc8 renews the blockade from the eighth rank.
Bf7 covers c4 and h5, restraining both pawns’ next advances.
Kc7 returns to keep b8 controlled. White can repeat the useful bishop placement.
Be6 again covers c8, c4 and h3. Black must change something.
h5 advances the h-pawn in the selected line.
Bf7 attacks h5 while maintaining control of c4.
h4 escapes the attack but is now one step from the bishop’s blocking square h3.
Be6 covers both h3 and c4, so either pawn advance becomes vulnerable.
c4 gives up the c-pawn rather than moving the king away from the blockade.
Bxc4 removes that pawn. Only h4 remains as a potential waiting move.
Kc8 maintains the blockade while the bishop is away from the checking diagonal.
Be6+ checks along e6-d7-c8, forcing the king off c8.
Kc7 returns to the remaining blockading square.
Bh3 blocks h4 and still controls c8 along h3-g4-f5-e6-d7-c8. Black must move the king away.
Kc6 is the illustrated retreat. With the pawn blocked, Black cannot simply wait.
Kb8 finally leaves the promotion square clear while keeping a7 defended.
Kb6 is the illustrated king continuation. It cannot prevent promotion on the next move.

Bd7+ offers the bishop and forces Black to respond to check.
Kxd7 takes it, but abandons control of b8.
Kb8 clears a8 and prepares promotion.
d4 advances in the illustrated source continuation; Black cannot stop a8=Q.

branches.title: Independent retreat through d8
commentary: This independent representative alternative begins after the same Bh3 blockade. It demonstrates why another king retreat also releases White’s king.
Kd8 abandons the square c7. Black cannot stay on c8 because the bishop controls it.
Kb8 clears the promotion square and maintains support of the pawn.
Ke8 is a representative legal king move, moving farther from the pawn.
a8=Q+ promotes with check along the eighth rank. The exact position is a White win.

exercises.prompt: Why does Bh3 finally release the white king?
exercises.answer: The bishop stops h4 from advancing and attacks c8. Black has no pawn move and cannot stay on c7, so the king must give ground and allow Kb8.

startContext: Begin after ...Kc8 at 54 seconds, a visually reconstructed seven-piece diagram. The earlier eight-piece Bf7 and ...Ba8 Kxa8 sacrifice remain source context. The selected full blockade route, d-pawn alternative and explicitly independent final king retreat are checked exactly.
